title: Someone I love has died
seoTitle: When Someone You Love Dies: Grief, Faith, and What Helps
description: When someone you love dies: what grief is really like, what the Bible says, what to do this week, when to get help, and how to help a friend.
summary: For the fog of the first weeks and the long year after: grief without hurry, honest prayer, and a hope that lets you cry.
askedAs: is it okay to be angry at God
answer: Someone you love has died, and the world did not have the decency to stop. Maybe it happened this week and you're signing papers in a fog, or maybe it was months ago and everyone else has moved on while you are still waking up to it. What you feel is not proof that something is wrong with you or your faith. It is love, still reaching for someone who isn't there. This page won't hurry you, and for tonight it is enough to tell one person you're not okay. If the grief has turned into not wanting to be here, I would rather you call or text one of the lines just below than read another word.
happening:
In the first days, grief often doesn't feel like sadness at all. It feels like shock, or like nothing. You make the calls, choose the casket or the urn, answer the same questions again and again, and part of you watches from far away. Many people are surprised by how physical it is: an exhaustion sleep doesn't touch, a weight on the chest, an appetite that vanishes, a fog that steals your keys and your words. Then the funeral ends, the relatives go home, and the house goes quiet. For many people, that is when grief truly begins.

It rarely moves in a straight line. It comes in waves that don't ask permission, a song in the grocery store or the moment you reach for the phone to tell them something. And you lose more than the person. You may lose the one who knew you first, the future you planned together, or the self you only were around them.

There are good explanations for all this, and each holds something true. Doctors will tell you grief is a normal response to loss, not an illness, and they're right. Many people half-remember the five stages of grief. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross first set them out in *On Death and Dying* (1969), from her work with patients facing their own deaths rather than with mourners, and she never meant them as a sequence everyone has to complete. Grieving people often feel what she named, but not on a schedule and not always in that order. And Christians will say your person is in a better place. For those who belong to Christ, Scripture does speak of being with him (Philippians 1:23), and that hope is no small thing. But each explanation leaves you out: still here, in a kitchen with their coffee cup in it, loving someone you can no longer reach.

Some losses carry a particular weight. The death of a child breaks the order of things, and grieving parents often find that even kind people don't know where to look. A death by suicide leaves grief tangled with questions that may never be answered, with guilt and anger, and often with a silence that makes it harder to speak of. A sudden death leaves no goodbye. After a long illness, relief can arrive beside the sorrow and feel like betrayal. And if the one who died was hard to love, or absent, you may grieve what you lost and what you never had. None of this means you are grieving wrong.

scripture.intro: Scripture doesn't rush the grieving or ask them to pretend. It gives you a shepherd in the valley, a Savior who wept at a grave, a psalm that ends in the dark, and a promise that death won't have the last word. Read these slowly, one a day if that's all you can manage.

passages.text: The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures; He leads me beside quiet waters. He restores my soul; He guides me in the paths of righteousness for the sake of His name. Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me; Your rod and Your staff, they comfort me. You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies. You anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows. Surely goodness and mercy will follow me all the days of my life, and I will dwell in the house of the LORD forever.
passages.reading: You've probably heard this psalm at a funeral, but it was written for the living. It bears David's name, and David kept his father's sheep before he was king, so he knew what a dark valley was to a sheep (1 Samuel 17:34-35). In the green pastures the psalm talks about God: “He makes me lie down” (Psalm 23:2). In the valley it starts talking to God: “You are with me” (Psalm 23:4). That is where it becomes a prayer. Even the table is spread with enemies still in the room, which is what grief is like: you are fed while death is still near, and the one who set the table stays.

passages.text: When Mary came to Jesus and saw Him, she fell at His feet and said, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” When Jesus saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, He was deeply moved in spirit and troubled. “Where have you put him?” He asked. “Come and see, Lord,” they answered. Jesus wept. Then the Jews said, “See how He loved him!”
passages.reading: Read the whole chapter when you can. Jesus waits two days after hearing that Lazarus is sick, and when he arrives his friend has been in the tomb four days. Martha meets him with words that sound close to blame, though she still says she trusts him, and instead of rebuking her he tells her, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11:25). When Mary falls at his feet with the same words, he explains nothing. He weeps. The word John uses for his being deeply moved carries an edge of indignation, and many readers have heard in it anger at death itself. Then he calls Lazarus out of the grave. The one person at that tomb who knew how the day would end cried anyway, so your tears are not unbelief. Your sentence, *if you had been here*, he has already heard twice.

passages.text: O LORD, the God of my salvation, day and night I cry out before You. ... My eyes grow dim with grief. ... Why, O LORD, do You reject me? Why do You hide Your face from me? ... You have removed my beloved and my friend; darkness is my closest companion.
passages.reading: Most psalms of lament turn toward praise before they end. This one closes with a beloved taken and darkness for company, and nothing after it to tie a bow on. The people of God kept it in their prayer book anyway, for nights like yours. It still opens by calling God “the God of my salvation” (Psalm 88:1), and it keeps crying out to him day and night, so even this prayer is an act of faith. Some nights you won't reach the end of Psalm 23. You can pray Psalm 88, tell God the truth, and go to bed.

passages.text: Brothers, we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope. For since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him.
passages.reading: Paul wrote to a young church in Thessalonica that had buried some of its own and seems to have feared the dead would miss the return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:15). The sentence is often quoted as if it said *do not grieve*. It doesn't. It says not to grieve like those without hope; the grief is assumed, and what changes is the direction it faces. Paul calls the dead those who sleep, the word Jesus used of Lazarus before he went to wake him (John 11:11), and a sleeper is someone you expect to see in the morning. Then he tells them to “encourage one another with these words” (1 Thessalonians 4:18). The hope is meant to pass gently from one grieving person to another.

passages.text: And I heard a loud voice from the throne saying: “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them. They will be His people, and God Himself will be with them as their God. ‘He will wipe away every tear from their eyes,’ and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain, for the former things have passed away.”
passages.reading: John saw this on the island of Patmos (Revelation 1:9), writing to seven churches, and in one of them a faithful witness named Antipas had already been killed (Revelation 2:13). It is the Bible's last word on grief, and it is more solid than the clouds we picture: John has just seen a new heaven and a new earth, and God comes down to live with his people. God will wipe away every tear, so there will still be tears when you arrive, and the hand that dries them will be his. Until then, mourning is the honest response to a world where death still has its hour.

whyHard:
Grief is hard because loss is hard, and no page can make it easy. But many grieving people carry a second weight on top of the first: the sense that they are doing it wrong, crying too long or too loudly or not enough. That weight comes from the world we have built around death, and the church helped build it.

For most of Christian history, people died at home, and a whole community knew what to do. Family and neighbors washed the body, sat up through the night, brought food, and dug the grave. Mourners wore black for months so strangers would know to be gentle, and late medieval Christians even wrote handbooks on dying well. Within a few generations most of that was gone. Dying moved into hospitals, the dead into funeral homes, and the funeral became a celebration of life, which can be beautiful but is a strange thing to require in the worst week of someone's life. We lost the customs that gave grief time and witnesses, and put nothing in their place.

The church absorbed the hurry and baptized it. We began treating composure as the evidence of faith, so the widow who doesn't cry at the funeral is praised for her strength and the one still crying at Christmas is handed a verse about joy. Our worship leans toward victory and leaves little room for lament. I'm a pastor, and pastors are among the worst offenders; we are trained to have a word ready, and it usually comes too soon. So grieving Christians decide their tears are a spiritual failure, and people outside the church decide Christianity has nothing to offer at a graveside but a greeting card.

C. S. Lewis learned the difference between an answer and a grief. Years before his wife Joy died in 1960, he had written *The Problem of Pain*, a careful argument about why a good God permits suffering. After her death he filled notebooks with something else: grief that felt like fear, and anger at a God who seemed to have gone silent. He published them in 1961 as *A Grief Observed*, under a pen name. The earlier book was true enough, and it could not reach him there.

Underneath the hurry is a belief about death itself. The modern world calls death natural, part of the circle of life, so grief must be a malfunction to manage. A certain kind of Christianity calls death a doorway, so grief must be a lack of faith. They sound like opposites and make the same mistake. Scripture calls death “the last enemy to be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 15:26), and grief is what love does in the presence of that enemy.

If you don't believe any of this, you may suspect the Christian hope is a story people tell to make death hurt less. I came to faith from atheism, so I won't wave that suspicion away, and Christians have sometimes used heaven exactly that way, as a painkiller. But a religion built only to comfort would never have kept Psalm 88 or given the world a Messiah who weeps at a funeral. Christianity agrees with what every grieving heart already says, that this is not how it was supposed to be, and it stakes that claim on an empty tomb you are free to examine.

So your tears are not the thing that went wrong. Death is. And the church, of all people, should be the last to hurry you past it.

thisWeek.intro: Grief can't be managed on a schedule, but it can be walked with small, faithful steps. Start with the first. If it's the only one you manage this week, that is enough.

steps.title: Let someone carry something
steps.body: Hand one or two people real tasks: the phone calls, the meals, the paperwork, the rides from the airport. People want to help and don't know how, so tell them, and tell one person the truth about how you're doing. Even Jesus asked his friends to stay and keep watch with him the night before he died (Matthew 26:38). If you can, put off big decisions like selling the house for now.

steps.title: Keep your body going
steps.body: Grief lives in the body. Drink water, eat something small even when you aren't hungry, step outside for a few minutes, and go to bed at the same time each night. Lower the bar for a good day to somewhere near the floor. If sleep has all but stopped or you're leaning on alcohol or pills, see a doctor and tell them about the death. Chest pain or trouble breathing is a reason to call 911 right away.

steps.title: Pray with borrowed words
steps.body: When you can't find words, borrow the Bible's. Read Psalm 23 or Psalm 88 aloud once a day and let it say what you can't. If all you can manage is their name and a groan, that is still prayer; the Spirit intercedes for us “with groans too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). Bring your anger too. God would rather hear the truth than polite silence.

steps.title: Keep their name and their stories
steps.body: Write down one memory a day, the more ordinary the better: how they answered the phone, what they always ordered, the thing they said too often. Say their name out loud, and ask the people close to you to say it too. Keeping the stories is not a failure to let go. It is how love keeps faith with a life.

steps.title: Mark the hard days before they come
steps.body: Put the dates on your calendar now: their birthday, your anniversary, the holidays, the day they died. Decide ahead of time who you'll be with and what you'll do, even if it's small: a visit to the grave, their favorite meal, a friend beside you at church. The first year is full of firsts, and the second year surprises many people, after everyone else has moved on.

moreHelp.body:
Grief is not an illness, and most grieving people don't need a diagnosis. They need time, people who stay, and freedom to be sad. But grief can grow heavier than a friend or a pastor can carry. A death by suicide, the death of a child, or a sudden or violent death more often needs skilled help, and so does grief that has kept you from functioning for months. A support group for people who lost someone the same way can help as friends can't; ask a hospice, a hospital chaplain, or your pastor where one meets. Seeing a counselor is no more a lack of trust in God than eating bread is.

Look for a licensed counselor who works with grief. Ask your doctor for a referral, search your insurance company's directory, or ask your pastor which counselors they trust. If you want a Christian counselor, ask for one, and either way confirm with your state's licensing board that they are licensed.
signs: You've had thoughts of ending your life or of not wanting to wake up. Call or text 988 now, or call 911 if you're in danger.
Months have passed and you still can't get up, eat, work, or care for your children.
You're using alcohol, pills, or anything else to get through the days or nights.
Chest pain or trouble breathing: call 911. Other symptoms that frighten you: see a doctor and mention the death.
Images of how they died replay until you can't sleep or function.
You feel nothing for a long time, or you've cut yourself off from everyone.
A child or teenager in the family is withdrawing, failing at school, or talking about wanting to die.
The estate, debts, or insurance are more than you understand. Talk to an attorney before you sign anything about them.
moreHelp.firstCall: You don't need the right words. You can say: *My father died in March. I'm not sleeping, I can barely work, and I don't know if this is normal grief.* Ask whether they're licensed in your state, whether they've worked with your kind of loss, what they charge, and whether they take your insurance or offer a sliding scale. If your faith matters to you, say so: *I'm a Christian, and I'd like that to be welcome here.* A good counselor won't mind the question.
moreHelp.cost: Help with grief doesn't have to be expensive. If your person was in hospice care, ask the hospice for grief support; a hospice certified by Medicare must make it available to the family for up to a year after the death. Ask churches and hospices near you about free grief groups. An employee assistance program at work may cover a few sessions, and community mental health centers and university training clinics often charge on a sliding scale. If the funeral left you in debt, tell your pastor; many churches keep a benevolence fund for needs like this.

helping.body:
If someone you love is grieving, you don't need the right words. You need to come, and to keep coming. In the first days, bring what they won't have to think about: a meal in a dish they never have to return, groceries, someone to answer the door. Instead of *let me know if you need anything*, which hands the work back to them, offer something specific and do it. Sit with them and let silence be fine. Job's friends did their best work in the first week, when “no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was” (Job 2:13). The trouble started when they began to explain.

Help pours in during the first weeks and dries up just as the house goes quiet, so keep calling. Say the name of the one who died; they haven't forgotten it for an hour. If the death was by suicide, don't ask how it happened, don't guess at why, and never suggest the person is at peace now. With children, use plain words like *died*; a phrase like *we lost him* can confuse a child. Pastors, learn the name, use it at the funeral, and call on the anniversary.
say: I'm so sorry. I don't know what to say, but I'm here.
Tell me about her. I'd love to hear.
I'm bringing dinner Thursday. Would six o'clock work?
I was thinking about your dad today.
I'll call you next week, too.
dontSay: At least you had him as long as you did.
I know exactly how you feel.
Shouldn't you be over this by now?
helping.next: Put the dates in your calendar now: the day of the death, their birthday, the first holidays, and the same dates next year. Call on those days, and keep inviting them even when they say no. If they talk about wanting to die or not wanting to be here, ask plainly whether they're thinking about suicide; asking does not put the idea in their head. Stay with them and help them call or text 988, or call 911 if they're in danger right now.

prayer:
Lord Jesus, you stood at your friend's grave and wept, though you knew what you were about to do. So I won't pretend with you.

The one I love is gone, and I don't know how to live without them. I'm tired in places sleep doesn't reach. Some days I'm angry with you, and you already know it. Some days I can't feel you at all. I'm not asking you to explain this tonight. I'm asking you not to leave.

Be my shepherd in this valley, because I can't see the way out. Keep count of my tears. Send people who will keep coming after the others stop, and on the nights when darkness feels like my closest companion, hold on to me when I can't hold on to you.

You have promised a morning when you will wipe every tear away and death will be no more. I can't feel that hope tonight. Hold it for me until I can. Amen.

faq.a: Longer than most people around you will expect, and not in a straight line. The sharpest pain usually softens into something you can carry, but grief for someone you loved doesn't simply end; it changes shape, and the second year surprises many people. Scripture sets no deadline on mourning. When Jacob believed his son was dead, “he refused to be comforted” (Genesis 37:35), and the Bible doesn't rebuke him. If months pass and you still can't function, see a doctor or a counselor. Needing that help doesn't mean you're grieving wrong.

faq.q: Is it okay to be angry at God?
faq.a: Yes, and you're in good company. The Psalms are full of believers who brought their anger straight to God: “How long, O LORD? Will You forget me forever?” (Psalm 13:1). When Lazarus died, both his sisters met Jesus with the same words, “Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died” (John 11:21), and he rebuked neither of them. Anger brought to God is still a way of talking to him. The real danger is anger that hardens into never speaking to him again.

Most Christians believe that those who belong to Christ are with him when they die; Paul called it being “away from the body and at home with the Lord” (2 Corinthians 5:8). But the final hope is not a soul drifting in the clouds. It is resurrection, bodies raised and the world made new, as the oldest creeds confess. That hope stands or falls on whether Jesus rose bodily from the grave, and Paul said plainly that “if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile” (1 Corinthians 15:17). It is a claim about history, and it is worth examining.

faq.q: Why are the holidays so hard after a death?
faq.a: Because the holidays are built around the people who are missing. The empty chair at Thanksgiving, the stocking no one fills, the song they always sang: the whole season points at the hole. Don't pretend it's a normal year. Decide ahead of time what you'll keep, what you'll skip, and who you'll be with, and give yourself permission to leave early. Some families set a place or light a candle. And remember that Advent itself is a season of waiting in the dark for a light that hasn't fully come.

faq.q: Is it normal to feel guilty after someone dies?
faq.a: It's very common: the last argument, the call you didn't return, a decision made at the hospital, the relief you felt when a long illness ended. Some guilt points at real wrongs, and those can be confessed and forgiven like any other. Much of it is love searching for a way it could have done more, and the relief is often love that could no longer bear to watch them suffer. If the death was by suicide, know that suicide rarely comes from any one thing and is not a verdict on your love. A counselor can help you sort what is true from what is torment.

If you were told that someone who dies by suicide is lost forever, you were told more than anyone can know. No one can pronounce on the eternal state of the person you love, and this page won't; that judgment belongs to God. Scripture never names suicide as a sin beyond forgiveness; the one sin Jesus calls unforgivable is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Mark 3:28-29). For centuries many Christians held suicide to be damning, because it takes a life that belongs to God and seems to leave no time to repent. Many others answer that no one dies with every sin confessed, and that salvation rests on what Christ has done. The Catholic Church, which calls the act gravely wrong, also teaches that anguish and fear can lessen a person's responsibility, that we should not despair of their salvation, and that the church prays for them. Every side can pray Abraham's question: “Will not the Judge of all the earth do what is right?” (Genesis 18:25). If this question has turned toward your own life, please call or text 988 now.

faq.q: How do you survive losing a child?
faq.a: Slowly, and not alone. The death of a child breaks the order of things, and no sentence makes it make sense, so be wary of anyone who offers one. Scripture doesn't. It records David's cry, “O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you” (2 Samuel 18:33), and it keeps Rachel “refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Jeremiah 31:15). The mother of Jesus stood near his cross (John 19:25). Find other parents who have buried a child; they can sit with you as others can't. Couples often grieve differently and can drift apart without meaning to, so ask for help early. Your other children are grieving too.

slots.note: James came to faith from atheism. In his own words, he could add what he believed about death before faith and what changed, beside the paragraph that answers the skeptic. The section stands without it.

Raised without a father, James could add a few sentences of his own on grieving a parent who was absent or hard to love, the grief for what never was. The last paragraph names this grief without his story.

How do you survive losing a child: as a father of five sons, James could add, in his own words, how that shapes the way he sits with parents who have buried a child. Nothing is assumed about his own losses.

Is suicide an unforgivable sin: where James lands, in his own words and from his own tradition. The answer as written states the positions fairly, says what Scripture does and does not say, and pronounces on no one.
If James wishes, what standing with families at funerals has taught him as a pastor, in his own words. The page invents no funerals, families, or conversations.

sources.claim: C. S. Lewis's wife Joy Davidman died in 1960, and his notebooks of grief were published in 1961 as A Grief Observed under the pen name N. W. Clerk.

sources.claim: Late medieval Christians wrote handbooks on dying well, the Ars moriendi texts of about 1415 and 1450.

The five stages were first set out by Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in On Death and Dying (1969), from interviews with terminally ill patients; she did not contend that everyone passes through each stage in sequence.
sources.cite: StatPearls (NCBI Bookshelf), Kubler-Ross Stages of Dying and Subsequent Models of Grief

sources.claim: Medicare-certified hospices must make bereavement services available to the family for up to one year after the patient's death.
sources.cite: 42 CFR 418.64(d)(1), Condition of participation: Core services (eCFR)

sources.claim: Asking someone directly whether they are thinking about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts or behavior.
sources.cite: National Institute of Mental Health, 5 Action Steps to Help Someone Having Thoughts of Suicide

sources.claim: The Catechism of the Catholic Church calls suicide gravely contrary to the just love of self (2281), teaches that grave psychological disturbance, anguish, or grave fear can diminish responsibility (2282), and teaches that we should not despair of the eternal salvation of those who have died by suicide and that the church prays for them (2283).

reviewed.notes: Second-pass review, 2026-09-29: truth, Scripture in context, theology, care, voice, links, and the four readers, in that order; validate-needs.mjs clean. Every outside claim was re-checked through search-engine excerpts of its named source (direct fetches are still blocked from this environment; re-open each before release): A Grief Observed published in 1961 under the pen name N. W. Clerk after Joy Davidman died in 1960; the five stages from On Death and Dying (1969), about dying patients, with Kübler-Ross denying they are a fixed sequence (StatPearls); Medicare-certified hospices must make bereavement services available to the family for up to a year (42 CFR 418.64(d)(1)); asking about suicide does not increase suicidal thoughts (NIMH); CCC 2281 to 2283. Truth and Scripture fixes: the stages sentence now names the book and says they were never meant as a required sequence, without claiming how often grief follows them; Psalm 23 is said to bear David's name rather than asserted as his; Martha's words are no longer called an accusation (she also says she trusts him, John 11:22); anger in John 11:33 is offered as a common reading, not a fact; the Thessalonians' fear is marked as inferred (4:15); Antipas is no longer generalized to all seven churches; 1961 added for A Grief Observed; the Ars moriendi claim now has a source. Care fixes: chest pain or trouble breathing now means 911, not a routine doctor visit; the suicide sign says now and adds 911; the child sign names talk of wanting to die, since talk about death is normal after a death; the hospice rule is stated exactly; no promise that a benevolence fund exists; 911 added to the helper's next step. The suicide FAQ now gives the historic view its real weight, the common answer to it, and the Catholic teaching fairly (including 2282 on diminished responsibility, and without 'even'); it pronounces on no one, says died by suicide, and ends with 988. 'Most Christians' for being with Christ at death. Voice: one of two Not X. Y. moves in Why this is so hard removed; a stock grief line and a doubled phrase rewritten. Links: every kit label checked against its target's real title; the plan label matches plans-index.json; the John 11 label no longer promises the whole story of Lazarus. /studyguides/grief and /studyguides/lament stay linked, and nothing on this page quotes or relies on their stories about James. The writer's choice to leave out /lament (the prophetic lament page on injustice) stands. Slots unchanged.
